chairs-have-reflected-the-technology-of-.title: "chairs have reflected the technology of their time"
chairs-have-reflected-the-technology-of-.content:
thoughts design
for a long time, i wondered why industrial designers are so obsessed with building chairs and lamps. i built some chairs and lamps of my own to try to find out. i have some mentors to thank for their guidance throughout this inquiry: Michael McNabb and Arthur O’Keefe from LaGuardia Community College’s Industrial Design program, and Tom Igoe from NYU ITP.
the answer that i’ve landed on is that it’s not purely about their function as a seat, or as a lighting fixture…
these objects are everywhere. everyone knows what a chair or a lamp should be, but an exploration investigates what they could be… it can be a personal exploration or an effort to push the boundary within the design field.
it’s about the fertile soil that these objects provide for exploration. they’re good prompts to start with so as to simplify the decision-making part so you don’t spend any more time wondering what to make. they can be very simple or as complex as you make them. the design and build process for chairs and lamps also forces you to practice a lot of valuable industrial design skills: concept development, sketching, CAD, prototyping, material exploration, fabrication, and documentation.
it’s just a bonus that they’re also functional!
examples of explorations:

building a chair to practice a woodworking technique that is new to you — personal
learning how to safely wire a lamp — personal
studying lighting theory and learning how to select the right lightbulb for your use-case — personal
trying new fabrication techniques such as large-scale 3d-printing — boundary-pushing
experimenting with new materials typically used in different contexts but novel to this field — boundary-pushing

designing-ai-interfaces.title: Designing AI Interfaces
designing-ai-interfaces.content:
books reading
Designing AI Interfaces: Design Principles for Creative and Autonomous AI by Louise Macfadyen
Foreword

“But there’s a meaningful difference between friction that wastes time and friction that prevents bad decisions.”


“as Henry Ford said, we’re in danger of inventing a faster horse when we should be inventing the car”


“the dominant AI UI (the textbox) aims for an appearance of authority and objectivity, AI outputs are not objective truths from infallible machines”

-> there is similar commentary about the false sense of objectivity in data, as mentioned in Data Feminism

“A model’s “93% confidence” is not a measurable accuracy like a spell-checker’s. Instead, it represents the probability of the next token in an unexplainable, high-dimensional space. Presenting this as a percentage is misleading; it’s a false precision that creates manufactured trust, rather than true transparency.”


“Perceived reliability and actual reliability can diverge entirely, and the gap is filled by whatever signal the interface sends during computation. That means the waiting state is a design surface, not an unavoidable tax.”


“the ELIZA effect: the natural human impulse to assume systems making humanlike language have human qualities”

1. Computation: Designing for the Processing and Generation Phase

“but in the AI era it goes beyond documenting needs or collecting feature requests: it means asking where users are likely to misinterpret, what signals will guide them toward the right understanding, and how much of the underlying process is worth revealing.”


“AI as what it is truly capable of being: a research assistant requiring partnership with human expertise and critical judgment.”


“real value as a tool for information retrieval, summarization, and drafting”


“Anthropic’s Claude models, which prioritize safety through constitutional AI training (a two-stage process that uses a set of principles called a “constitution” instead of human feedback to train AI models);”


“In their 2021 paper “On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots”, researchers Emily Bender, Angelina McMillan-Major, Timnit Gebru, and Margaret Mitchell warned that the race to build ever-larger models risked overlooking crucial issues: these systems could amplify biases present in their training data, consume massive amounts of energy with environmental consequences, and create the illusion of understanding while merely recombining patterns from their training corpus.”

2. Output: Designing the Delivery and Presentation of LLM Responses

“Do prompts decay, do outputs get versioned”


“Cost per pageload isn’t a commonly surfaced consideration in product design. An app can make dozens of third-party API calls—payment processing, address validation, image recognition, and so on—but these usually result in a stable, definable cost.”


“interfaces often use lightweight cues like natural language commands (“search the web for…”) or syntax hints (“@web” or “/search”) to give experienced users precise control.”


“Frameworks like the Model Context Protocol (MCP) formalize how a tool describes its capabilities, what information it requires, and how that information should be structured so the model can use it. You can think of this as a simplified API that is specialized for use by models.”


“The challenge with automatic routing lies in transparency and user agency. If a choice is made invisibly, users may not understand why responses vary in speed, style, or capability across different queries. A small badge persistently displaying the model and its benefits helps users understand why a response might take longer or have access to different types of information.”


“Many current efforts are focused on creating new benchmarks that better reflect open-ended use, long-form reasoning, or more dynamic tasks like planning and tool use”


“designers frequently report that it is “difficult to grasp what AI can or cannot do,” which as a result “hampers designers’ brainstorming and sketching processes from the start.””


“This ambient information shapes interpretation in ways that the typed request alone cannot. The same instruction, issued in a different context, might produce an entirely different result.”

3. Designing for AI Inputs

“This recurrent optimization behavior reflects the knowledge gained in the nearly 25 years since Google launched: how to structure a good query for Google. And it’s exactly this knowledge that users don’t yet have for AI products.”


“implicit context: the information a system gathers from the environment without being asked. Examples include the document currently open, the text a user has selected, their location, the time of day, and what they did moments ago. There is explicit prompting: the typed or spoken request that tells the system what to do. And there is direct manipulation: the sliders, selections, buttons, and gestures that let users shape AI behavior through familiar interface patterns. A single interaction might involve all three”


“The command-line interface (CLI) represented a world where the burden of communication rested entirely on the human participant, demanding that users translate their goals into the computer’s preferred vocabulary through extensive documentation, training, and practice.”

itp/automatons/index.title: Automatons
itp/automatons/index.content:
Fabricating Mechanical Automatons (Batteries Not Included) taught by Josh Corn
Course Description:

How do we make things move, produce sounds, or maybe even emit light without batteries? Through this course, each student will design their own purely mechanical automaton. We will learn how to use simple materials and tools to hand prototype mechanisms in their early stages. Various software tools will be used to refine the designs and then a series of traditional and digital fabrication tools (various wood shop tools, laser cutter, 3D printers, etc.) will be used to produce the final pieces. We will learn how to work iteratively in the shop through weekly exercises and a final project.

itp/creative-computing/index.title: Creative Computing
itp/creative-computing/index.content:
Creative Computing taught by Carrie Sijia Wang
I am the Graduate Assistant (GA) for this course.
Course Description:

In this course students will be asked to think beyond conventional applications of computation to explore creative and expressive possibilities through code. Students will learn the fundamentals of programming as they build interactive projects using p5.js, a JavaScript library designed for creative coding. Through exercises on coding fundamentals (variables, conditionals, iteration, functions and objects), students will gain a deeper appreciation of computation’s expressive potential as they learn to author their own software, and not simply use that which has been provided to them. The course will then cover a variety of applications of computation including interactive sound synthesis and audio visualization, image manipulation and processing, data visualization, and machine learning integration with ml5.js. Additional topics  include working with APIs to access real-time data, web development fundamentals, and experimental coding approaches and generative development tools. Structured weekly exercises are aimed at building specific skills in each domain, however students are free to pursue their own diverse interests as they combine these techniques in their midterm and final projects.

itp/efl/index.content:
Endless Frontier Labs taught by Deepak Hegde
Course Description:

The MBA CLASS offers a unique opportunity to learn about selecting, managing, and financing scalable startups through interactions with early-stage science and tech companies and their investors. It is ideal for students pursuing careers in entrepreneurship, innovation, venture capital, and new product development. The class is part of the nine-month Endless Frontier Labs program, one of the world’s most selective accelerators for startups in breakthrough science and technologies.

itp/efl/week-1.title: week 1
itp/efl/week-1.content:
readings

How VC’s Make Decisions (see class Brightspace page)
Should Investors Bet on the Jockey or the Horse?
Are “Better” Ideas More Likely to Succeed

How VC’s Make Decisions
tl;dr jockey (team) > horse (business/strategy)
deal sourcing & selection

generating deal flow: VCs connecting with start-ups that are looking for funding
VCs rely on their networks to source opportunities

entrepreneurs should research who belongs to a VC’s network and try to get an introduction from someone in it
because management team weighs so heavily in investment decisions, entrepreneurs who are not plugged into venture networks may face hurdles


for VCs, having a clear message about what you will and will not do, how you provide real venture assistance, and how you approach bold visions is key to winning these types of opportunities
how VCs deliver alpha (in order of importance):

deal sourcing — most critical
deal selection
post-investment actions



jockey vs. horse

jockey = entrepreneurial team
horse = start-up’s strategy and business model
strength of founding team is more important than the start-up’s strategy or business model
what contributes most to success/failure of portfolio companies: management team — most critical

term sheet structure
typical VC term sheets ensure the entrepreneur will do very well financially if they perform, but investors can take control of the business if the entrepreneur doesn’t deliver:

cash flow rights — the financial upside that gives founders incentives to perform
control rights — the board and voting rights that allow VCs to intervene if needed
liquidation rights — the distribution of the payoff if the company flounders and has to be sold
employment terms, particularly vesting — gives entrepreneurs incentives both to perform and stay at the company

investment terms critical to VCs

pro rata investment rights — allow VCs to acquire an additional stake in a company and preserve their initial ownership percentage in subsequent rounds

“the biggest source of returns is our ability to double down on our winners”


liquidation preferences
antidilution rights
vesting of the founders’ equity
company’s valuation
board control — seen as the most important control mechanism

glossary

IRR (internal rate of return): only calculated after the fact, when there is an exit for our limited partners
antidilution rights: allow the number of shares that current investors hold to be adjusted if future financing rounds are done at a lower price than the current round
liquidation rights: ensure that if a company is sold, the VCs get paid before the founders do; typically guarantee the amount invested or some multiple of it (e.g., double)
option pool: an amount of equity set aside for grants to compensate current and future employees of the start-up; usually a percentage of the company’s total value
participation rights: allow VCs to get back the face value of their investment (or a multiple of it), then share in the value created above that level at the time of a company exit
pro rata investment rights: give VCs the right to invest in a company’s subsequent investment rounds and preserve their initial percentage of ownership
redemption rights: give VCs the ability to return stock to the company — i.e., force it to pay back the amount of the investment

universities as a source of deal flow

universities are often the source of innovations that end up in the portfolios of VCs
university officials can learn how to better leverage the innovative activity happening within their halls
building relationships with leading VCs and promoting an entrepreneurial community can help spur start-up activity


Should Investors Bet on the Jockey or the Horse?
tl;dr jockey (team) < horse (business/strategy)

examines how VC-backed companies evolve from early business plan -> IPO -> public company
core implication for jockey-vs-horse debate: investors in start-ups should place more weight on the business (“the horse”) than on the management team (“the jockey”), since businesses tend to stick while management gets swapped along the way

paper’s actual data: management turnover is common, but business lines almost never change; horse stays put and jockey is routinely swapped out

a good business can survive bad management getting replaced, but a bad business rarely gets saved by a great team





Are “Better” Ideas More Likely to Succeed? An Empirical Analysis of Startup Evaluation
tl;dr horse > jockey holds especially well in R&D-intensive sectors, precisely because those businesses coalesce early around IP/technology. in sectors without that hard IP anchor, the “horse” is much less legible early on.
core finding: it depends on the sector

in R&D-intensive sectors (life sciences, hardware, energy): ideas that got more mentor interest were significantly more likely to reach commercialization and raise real funding

why? tend to form around concrete, hard-to-change intellectual assets (patents, academic research, core technology) — the idea itself is the critical resource, so it’s assessable on paper
careful upfront screening of the idea itself is worthwhile — the fixed costs of getting it wrong are high, and the idea is diagnostic


in non-R&D-intensive sectors (consumer web/mobile, enterprise software, consumer products): mentor interest had basically no predictive power at all — reading the idea alone told you nothing about whether it would succeed

why? form more around the founders’ human capital and pivot/adapt heavily as they go — so an early idea summary doesn’t capture what the company will actually become
upfront idea-screening doesn’t tell you much — a “spray and pray” approach (small bets, let it play out) or vetting the founding team may be more efficient, since the business will likely look very different by the time it succeeds

itp/eccentric-engineering/index.title: Eccentric Engineering
itp/eccentric-engineering/index.content:
Eccentric Engineering taught by Tega Brain
Course Description:

Critical design uses the language and tools of design to ask questions rather than solve problems. It makes the familiar strange, renders the invisible legible, and proposes alternatives not because they are convenient but because imagining them, and building them, changes what is seen as possible. This course draws methods from this tradition, but applies them to networked infrastructure and engineering, what we will call eccentric engineering. Not engineering as optimization, but engineering as argument. The working hypothesis is that the most powerful design works do not just reveal broken systems but are themselves systems that run differently. This course is about critically engaging with function, and implementing critique through new propositions.
The course moves through three modes: reading infrastructure, defamiliarizing infrastructure through making, and proposing alternates. The environmental dimension of this topic is the ground condition from which everything else follows. Computation is infrastructure, it is a physical thing embedded in a material, living world, and yet it is mostly designed as if it isn’t. How might things be different?

itp/eccentric-engineering/week-1.title: week 1
itp/eccentric-engineering/week-1.content:
Homework

READ: The Critical Engineering Manifesto - Julian Oliver, Gordan Savičić, Danja Vasiliev.
READ: Langdon Winner, “Do Artifacts Have Politics?”
READ (OPTIONAL): Dean Chahim, “Engineers Don’t Solve Problems” (Logic(s) Magazine, Issue 5: Failure, 2018)
WRITE and POST your responses to these readings. Consider how Winner’s ideas translate to the system of infrastructure you have chosen to think through in your class response. What designed characteristics in your system are normalized and therefore taken for granted? Who or what does it exclude or include?
FIND a work or example of eccentric or critical engineering and make a post with an image, link and write a sentence or two describing its methods


Reading Notes
The Critical Engineering Manifesto - Julian Oliver, Gordan Savičić, Danja Vasiliev.
criticalengineering.org/ resonance

treat the technologies we depend upon as objects of study, suspicion and intervention
“2. The Critical Engineer raises awareness that with each technological advance our techno-political literacy is challenged.”
“7. The Critical Engineer observes the space between the production and consumption of technology. Acting rapidly to changes in this space, the Critical Engineer serves to expose moments of imbalance and deception.”
“10. The Critical Engineer considers the exploit to be the most desirable form of exposure.”
the critical design engineering manifesto (remixed)
“3. The Critical Design Engineer designs seams — not seamlessness — so the user can understand, configure, and contest.”
“6. The Critical Design Engineer knows that ‘agent’ describes socio-technical dynamics involving models, parameters, tokens, reinforcement loops, protocols, products, networks, devices and bodies”
“8. The Critical Design Engineer looks to the history of critical design, speculative design, adversarial design and their discontents, and carries their strategies out of the gallery and into the repository, where critique must survive contact with use.”


Langdon Winner, “Do Artifacts Have Politics?”
(OPTIONAL): Dean Chahim, “Engineers Don’t Solve Problems” (Logic(s) Magazine, Issue 5: Failure, 2018)

Assignment
Critical Annotation and Intervention Assignment (10%)

You are to select one piece of infrastructure that you interact with daily — a router, a platform, a web protocol, a data center visible on a map, a water pipe, a tap. Trace your chosen infrastructure’s actual physical and administrative path: where does it originate and who or what does it flow onto, who maintains it, what standards govern it, who pays, who is excluded, what ecological costs it displaces, and what does it conceal? What does it do when it functions perfectly? What does this show us about its ideal operation?
Identify when the infrastructure normally “disappears” – i.e., when it works so well no one notices it – and the moment it breaks down and suddenly becomes visible (a blackout, a breakage, a service outage, slowness). What does this reveal about the characteristics of its ideal operation? What political or economic decision is this breakdown moment actually revealing? Who bears the cost when it fails, and who bore the cost when it was built?
Create an intervention that engages with this system exposing an invisible assumption within it or that suggests how it might behave differently. For example:


Deliberately misuse it, or use it in the wrong way. Document your efforts.
Design a counter-measuring device that tracks and displays a hidden dynamics, impacts or costs of the system
A protocol or governance document — a fictional-but-plausible RFC, zoning amendment, or maintenance manual for an alternative version of the system, written with the same bureaucratic seriousness as the real thing
A deliberately inefficient or “wrong” version of the system that restores something optimization erased

Create and annotate a diagram of your system with your findings from (1) and (2) along with some documentation or diagramming of your intervention for (3).

itp/friction-by-design/index.title: Friction by Design
itp/friction-by-design/index.content:
Friction by Design: A Critical AI Studio taught by Louise Macfadyen
Course Description:

AI products have inherited decades of dark patterns engineered to capture attention, increase addiction, and extract value. This studio names the social impact of those patterns and asks students to design against them. Taught by Louise Macfadyen, author of Designing AI Interfaces (O’Reilly, 2026), the course grounds students in the best practices of AI product design and engineering, and equips them to build interfaces that engage honestly with the tensions those patterns create.
The weekly practice pairs building with (light) critical reading. We’ll read Natasha Dow Schüll on the design of the casino, Cory Doctorow on enshittification, dark-pattern taxonomies, and recent case studies on chatbot-induced delusion. To aid students in constructing interrogative studies, we’ll juxtapose these readings with approaches from contemporary art that sought to evade consumerization — reviewing the de-objectification practices of the 1960s and 70s through the work of artists like Yoko Ono and George Brecht.
Each week pairs one of these readings with a building exercise. Students will practice translating design specs into functional web prototypes using LLM-assisted coding (sometimes called “vibe coding”), treating each prototype as a test of whether a critique survives contact with a built object - and revising accordingly. Take-home exercises invite students to prototype experiments in adding friction and counter-patterns. In-class exercises cover design engineering best practices alongside model-behavior tools like fine-tuning and evals, equipping students to create digital “studies” that probe AI directly. By the end of the term, students will have built a working vocabulary - and a working portfolio - of friction as an implementable design tool.

itp/nime/index.title: NIME
itp/nime/index.content:
New Interfaces for Musical Expression taught by David Rios
Course Description:

In this course students create digital musical instruments and do a live performance using them. Over the semester, we look at examples of current work by creators of musical interfaces, and discuss a wide range of issues facing technology-enabled performance – such as novice versus virtuoso performers, discrete versus continuous data control, and the relationship between musical performance and visual display. Readings and case studies provide background for class discussions on the theory and practice of designing controllers for musical performance. Students design and prototype a musical instrument – a complete system encompassing musical controller, algorithm for mapping input to sound, and the sound output itself. A technical framework for prototyping performance controllers is made available. Students focus on musical composition and improvisation techniques as they prepare their prototypes for live performance. The class culminates in a musical performance where students (or invited musicians) will demonstrate their instruments

The course aims to teach the technical and artistic aspects of Projection Mapping, enabling the creation of immersive and experiential art installations. The focus extends beyond acquiring the necessary technical skills for producing Projection Mapping works; it also emphasizes the effective use of the medium to bring concepts to life. Encompassing various types of projection mapping, such as outdoor mobile projection, interactive wall, and holographic projection, the curriculum encourages students to experiment with the medium as much as possible. The goal is to produce work that authentically represents each artist and achieves a harmonious balance between art and the technologies they employ.

First assignment
Create a short (4 min) presentation that introduces you and your interests, and post it using this form.
1. Look back Take some time to reflect on what you’ve made and learned at ITP so far. Which projects have been your favorites? Which were the most interesting or challenging? Prepare a few slides to share with the class. You’re welcome to include work or experiences from before ITP, or from your life outside ITP, if they feel relevant. Tip: Keep the slides simple. A quick sequence of four slides with one image each is easier to follow than four images crowded onto a single slide.
2. Look for connections As you review your projects and experiences, consider:

Do you notice any common threads?

- Are there projects you’d like to continue developing?
- Are there themes or questions you’d like to explore further—or move away from?
For your final slide, choose a word, short phrase, image, diagram, or other simple visual that captures your current hunch about where your interests might be heading.
A few things to keep in mind:
This isn’t meant to be a polished final product, but a starting point. The goal is to begin reflecting on your interests and share them with the group so we can start getting to know each other.
You’ll have only 4 minutes, so please practice ahead of time and time yourself.

rebecca-black.title: Rebecca Black
rebecca-black.content:
thoughts critical haterpee
yesterday, rebecca black’s “friday” resurfaced on my social media feed. it was worse than i remembered. when it came out in 2011, i remember watching it with my cousins and talking about it with uncle thai.
uncle thai said:

“this girl knows how to sing, but she has no talent for it.”

rebecca came from a well-off family, with both parents being veterinarians. they paid ARK Music Factory $4000 for the music video. presumably, she also had singing lessons to learn the techniques for singing, but her innate voice ends up not being pleasant to listen to. now, she is a DJ who has performed at Boiler Room.
this reminded me of my ex boyfriend whose wealthy parents, even wealthier than black’s, bankrolled each and every one of his short films. i liked him a lot but the writing of his films reeked of being soulless, out-of-touch, and spiritually chopped… makes sense when you had such a sterile and privileged upbringing— no character.
people like that get to LARP as an artist or director without having to build their way up working as a PA or intern, or save up their own money. it’s easier to fail upward when you have a portfolio crediting yourself as someone who produced all of these works involving big crews and resources— most people don’t have that opportunity— inevitably, you stand out. it just goes to show how unmeritocratic these industries are.
realization:

shit, i was dating the male chinese equivalent of rebecca black.

as i mentioned in discussions on rich people and art, me being salty enough about this to write about it definitely is a form of passivity in disguise. but at the same time it motivates me to work harder. weird.
there is a funny comment my friend MT makes when a rich person pisses them off:

“they’re dying first in the revolution!”

clown-workshop.title: clown workshop
clown-workshop.content:
experiences
i went to a life-changing clown (improv) workshop in some dude’s basement with my friend Ashley Sun. i had no idea what to expect going in. it was 3-hours long and began with everyone doing a 1-minute solo improv performance, and built up to everyone doing 5-minute performances by the end.
the instructor prefaced it as “letting out your inner child”, but for me, i viewed it as “letting out your inner animal”.
from an outsiders’ perspective listening into what was going on in the basement, it probably sounded like we were having an orgy or something. yelling, animal noises, crying, rolling and tumbling around.
social constructs and an urban landscape repress us in ways we’re not even fully aware of. so, it was nice to have this safe space full of kind (but weird) people to just let it all go.
i don’t think i’m the same person after this workshop.

everything-wrong-with-america.title: everything wrong with america
everything-wrong-with-america.content:
drafts writing critical haterpee
some unstructured thoughts about american consumerism and capitalism.
08-10-2026
barbara kruger’s “i shop therefore i am” and its elegant critique of american consumerism
my white american roommate, who to me, represents all that is wrong with america: neoliberalism, individualism, yellow-fever/fetishization of asian culture as an aesthetic, materialism, consumerism, a lack of hobbies besides consumerism, whiteness-as-default, instagram-story-trend-hopping masked as having political views, superiority complex from having an urban yuppy bullshit consulting job.
premium mediocre experiences
bullshit jobs
11-09-2025
I hate white america
(disclaimer: i am a yuppie transplant with a significant amount of privilege that allows me to live, work, and study in a place like new york city.)
i’m convinced that those who subscribe to the neoliberal, capitalistic and individualistic culture that exists in america don’t and may never experience what community could be. how can you? when the way you grow up is exactly as the “american dream” pushes: nuclear family with 1-2 kids, behind a white picket fence in a car-dependent suburb, “friends” and family we hardly see because they’re too busy tending to their individual lives to even be depended on to drive you to the airport. a lot of kids i’ve met from affluent backgrounds who didn’t get to grow up in big extended families or ethnic enclaves don’t know how to properly share. especially in white america, it leads to a personality shaped around consumerism to compensate for a lack of culture, leading to a over-emphasis of ownership of material objects… “what’s mine and what’s yours”. it’s sad that in Vietnam, they often view Vietnamese-Americans as people who have “lost their roots”. i don’t disagree, in a lot of ways i feel white-washed too and now i wish i could somehow undo it.
i don’t mean to romanticize living in community either. there are points where with my family, and in Vietnam, that i struggle to have privacy or independent thought, because it constantly feels like people are projecting their opinions and voices in my ears.
in a way, keeping others at arm’s reach feels like avoidance. it’s safer to people-please and remain at the surface level. there’s not enough time nor energy in a day to ruffle any feathers. conflict is scary!!! here, we’d rather be lonely than learn how to compromise.
i remember when i was in middle school and trying to do my homework in my bedroom while my parents were loudly singing karaoke in the other room. i complained to Uncle Thai and he admonished me, sharing his experience of having immigrated to america at my age as a part of a family of 7, squished into a government-subsidized studio apartment in washington, dc, with only enough room to lay out several mattresses on the floor, where everyone slept and spent time together. there was no privacy, but they survived. this moment taught me that there are times that you have to compromise for community.
i don’t mean to glorify their struggle either. i think their circumstances inhibited them in some ways. for instance, a lot of my family members shit on the same Uncle Thai for doing poorly in school. but how could he have done well without having a quiet place, or a proper desk to study at home? but the same circumstances that they struggled through, together as a family allowed them to remain close to this day.
new york city and other forms of privilege
new york city causes you to objectify other people. whether in dating where people and interactions are gamified into swipes on a screen, or people you call friends coming and going, whether its from being “too busy” or literally moving away. it often feels like you have to be an asshole because kindness somehow gets interpreted as a sign that you’re a pushover. in the train stations, we are conditioned to ignore homeless people. it’s not an unusual sight to witness people overdosing on the street. it’s sad to have become so desensitized to the normalization of… human beings’ suffering.
(disclaimer again: i am a yuppie transplant with a significant amount of privilege that allows me to live, work, and study in a place like new york city.)
i find a lot of my kind (lol) to be largely performative and i’m still trying to process how i feel about it. i find it really difficult to take people seriously when they move to a place for not even a year, live in an ivory tower high-rise doorman building, hang out exclusively with people from their private school alma mater and tax-bracket, and post profusely on their instagram story about nyc politics. to simultaneously exist in a bubble and to pretend to be mad about class and inequality makes no sense to me. i find that the biggest yappers and virtue-signalers are not the ones out there canvassing for or donating to [insert the currently trending political candidate here]‘s campaign. no, they’re way too busy!!! …going to marketing pop-up events to get free shit that ends up taking up even more space in an overflowing apartment with all the other hoarded junk and buying $9 matcha (it’s me! i’m a hypocrite. i’m disgusted at myself). it really is disgusting the way that Americans treat their homes as storage units rather than a home with intention and utility and space to walk around in the storage room. it’s exhausting to live with these karens and NIMBYs-in-training where you’re made to feel like you have to negotiate for every inch of space just because they had been there first. (history really repeats itself because that’s the same rhetoric the yts use, totally ignoring what they did to the native americans) and they don’t even see the power imbalances in these situations.
obligatory white ppl rant
i think that white americans like my roommate are so unaware of just how much space they take up figuratively and literally. from dominating conversations and being condescending to BIPOC who don’t conform to their idea of whiteness being the baseline for the default or “the norm” (can you imagine if all BIPOC conformed to white as the norm? that would be the most tasteless, bland, boring, and flat reality to live in) or what’s acceptable or literally the sheer amount of consumerism and materialistic bullshit that their culture encourages them to engage in. they like to act like the police officers of the world, which america has a history of doing (ahem, theodore roosevelt, big stick diplomacy, panama, ahem). white americans don’t understand just how laughable their ‘history’ and their ‘culture’ is. it’s clearly not a model for other countries, just look at the obesity and education stats in this place; it’s rough out here. the one that’s the most embarrassing but the one that lacks humility the most, going further with being self-aggrandizing, self-victimizing, subscribing to the snowflake-participation-trophy-culture that expects constant external validation from others for accomplishing little to nothing. i know that the way to get on people’s good side here i have to praise them when they say shit like “you know what, i’m so proud of how far i’ve come” like a line from a shitty coming-of-age movie, and it’s my own fault for rejecting it and coming across as rude in their eyes. it’s hard to respect someone when this country socialized them into an agent of white supremacy.
they try to defend themselves because maybe they have some BIPOC friends, but again, those friends are often white-washed to be able to put up with the whiteness.
i find that the only enjoyable white people to be around are the ones who have significantly distanced themselves from the american corporate neoliberal individualistic materialistic machine and have freed themselves from their whiteness through art or spirituality or whatever. ones who are not spiritually chopped.
if america never intervened in the vietnam war (which the vietnamese actually refer to as “the american war”) then my family would’ve never had to uproot our lineage and end up here lol. i often hate it here and have to put in great effort to find things to like. i never asked to be here, but pragmatically it doesn’t make sense to leave at this stage in my life. my family and roots are here. love and hate—two truths can exist at the same time, but like with a lot of things, this country struggles with nuance.
an ex-boyfriend once commented that i’m “racist toward white people”. lol. but i argue that white americans are racist every day, most of the time not even intentionally, but due to sheer ignorance. even when they claim to enjoy aspects of other cultures— their attempts end up half-baked and more often than it’s appropriation at best. i’m looking at the asiaboos. i’m also looking at my fallen asian brothers and sisters with a high proximity to whiteness (white-washing lol, WAKE UP). i pour one out for the ones who end up as the token asian/non-white in an all-white friend group because i know they’re going through some form of self-loathing that makes them wish they were white, too. surely, with the token white in an asian friend group (the asiaboo), the white one doesn’t wish they were asian.
like julia lee in “biting the hand: growing up asian in black and white america”, i am angry, a lot. what society collectively needs to heal is for white people to stop acting up.
what this book has to say about “reverse-racism”:

Racial minorities have not historically held systemic power in Western societies like the United States.
Individual acts of prejudice by a minority person against a white person do not equate to the centuries of historical, systemic oppression and institutional marginalization that people of color have faced.
The term “reverse racism” is often used to distract from or deflect conversations about systemic racism and racial equity initiatives.

racism is a function of prejudice + institutional power
in practicing “humanizing the enemy” and empathy, what often goes through my head when i have a conflict is “aw, i guess they can’t help that they’re so white.” …for better or for worse. but it’s what keeps me sane and allows me to move on from the stupid ass shit they say and do.
something insidious is when rather than acknowledging their own privilege they grasp at straws to try to find it in others. unprompted, so quick to try to lower others with “it’s such a privilege you get to attend grad school” maybe you could attend too, if you planned ahead, saved your money and you stopped buying Tik Tok Shop-Temu-Teso Life junk? this shit is not free. it’s suuuch a privilege to dig into my 3+ years of savings to pay this exorbitant tuition to this private, morally ambiguous institution. shit, am i upholding white supremacy by attending here?
other thoughts on privilege…
university is a place for laundering privilege… meritocracy is fake… (parents’) fortune favors the brave. these are thoughts that have made me feel really frustrated but i guess i’ve improved in the sense that i don’t allow them to ruin my day as much as they once did.
we’re all gentrifiers here, this is a city built upon invading and displacing people. it’s definitely not good, but it’s a difficult truth that we shouldn’t try to avoid. even the native americans technically immigrated here on the land bridge. there’s no need to push that the owner at the nearby bodega has finally learned your name to validate that you’re a “real new yorker”, that you’re “not a gentrifier”, that you’re somehow better than those white gentrifiers living down the hall from you in your overpriced building. we’re all cosplaying in this city that’s cosplaying as what it used to be.
america, and probably the world, is doomed if we keep down this path of 100% remote bullshit jobs. we can’t be attempting to find meaning in our material objects and premium mediocre consumption. but sometimes shelling out your wages for the sake of signaling taste and striving in the food you eat without requiring deep knowledge or being genuinely luxury items is fun and makes you feel like you’re somehow better than those who don’t care <3.
this became a rant. i’m probably a people-hater with a superiority complex.

family-lore.title: family lore
family-lore.content:
family thoughts
01-30-2024
My dad was sent away to live at another’s family’s home as a carpentry apprentice when he was 15 years old. he had to do work on their house and farm in exchange for a place to stay.
my grandma once had an infection after getting her tooth removed. she asked around the village and family/friends and no one wanted to even loan money. my dad had to send money home to help out.
if he were to come to the US at an earlier age, he probably would’ve gone to college. he’s a lot more disciplined and smarter than i am. he consistently ranked first in his school exams but our family wasn’t able to afford his education past middle school. it’s a waste.
he said he dreamed to enlist as a navy officer to give back to his family and to the US, the country that allowed my family to leave Vietnam, where we would’ve probably died in poverty because my grandpa fought on the losing side of the war.
my grandpa was a prisoner of war for 5 years. 5 YEARS!!!
it’s crazy to imagine how even in the US, how close my family was to poverty, from having everything taken away from us by corruption, to where we are now.
Dad expressed that because he’s been through so much struggle, he’s able to put up with any struggle in his life now to take care of his family. Because anything now is better than back then.

just-vibe-coding-won't-get-you-a-job.title: just vibe-coding won't get you a job
just-vibe-coding-won't-get-you-a-job.content:
quotes thoughts ai drafts

“Understanding software fundamentals allows you to recognize what tradeoffs even exist.”
— Andrew Ng

I agree. In this age of vibe-coding, I don’t think it’s as necessary to be adept in lower-level systems programming or syntax, but it’s still important, and perhaps even more important, to study software architecture, design patterns, existing off-the-shelf/open-source solutions to understand the tradeoffs, not constantly be reinventing the wheel, write better prompts, and effectively make better decisions. especially with how every AI prompt costs tokens with financial, environmental, and societal costs that have been heavily abstracted away from our daily view.
What sets apart an experienced software engineer from a novice is the ability to understand the bigger picture of the software they’re building— knowing how to go beyond the MVP/POC and optimize, whether that’s for performance, latency, saving compute costs, etc.
When I was working at IBM doing data engineering and machine learning, the key to getting promoted was not simply writing better code. It was being able to draw software and cloud architecture diagrams for the products we were selling and explain them to stakeholders, and to be able to justify decisions made in the software design.

Stuff like this was my bread and butter that kept me employable at the time.
I think the best ways to learn these skills are to:

Work in a software job that requires you to collaborate on a large codebase with a team
Work on open-source projects that require you to make pull requests
Work on a longterm personal project where you are regularly committing to GitHub, sharing with real-world users, collecting feedback, and delivering improvements and bug fixes
General curiosity about how the things you’re building work, rather than just accepting whatever Claude Code throws at you.
Read the following: “Designing Data-Intensive Applications” by Martin Kleppmann, “Fundamentals of Data Engineering” by Joe Reis, “Designing AI interfaces” by Louise Macfadyen, “Designing Machine Learning Systems” by Chip Huyen, Design Patterns (FYI, these books are all free if you log into O’Reilly using your NYU email!)

Note: if you’re spending all of your time reading and not really writing code, then you’re just LARPing and not actually learning



Overall, the computer science degree is still really useful. Anyone who says that it’s pointless to study CS because of AI is fear-mongering and doesn’t know what they’re talking about. It’s only pointless to study CS for the people who go through the motions and get their degree without actually learning anything. But if you do it right, it’s an invaluable skillset to, at some level, understand how computers and OS’s work, how networks work, data structures and algorithms, optimization and the math involved, networks and cloud architecture, etc. Of course this background is going to give you a leg up, especially with vibe-coding. (See below for what Andrew Ng had to say about how it helps you give coding agents better context.)

But at the same time, if you didn’t study CS, you’re not necessarily cooked either. There’s a lot of types of work out there that you just need to open your mind to.

Just vibe-coding MVPs, web art, POCs for yourself isn’t going to get you there.
To my peers at ITP/IMA,

making art with code with p5.js and some HTML/CSS
VS.
software engineering as a profession that will make you money and pay your bills
are two very different things.

Not saying that one is better than the other. But it’s important to understand the differences to align your expectations to the path you want to follow, whether it’s as a creative technologist, design engineer, HCI researcher, etc. To be realistic in your job search, just accept that you can’t do it all, a spray-and-pray approach isn’t effective. It’s better to be focused and selective from the start. (More on this with careering.) Wouldn’t you rather be good at one or a few things rather than be mediocre at many things?
The main thing is to view AI tools more as a collaborator rather than a solution, and to get your hands dirty and constantly be breaking and fixing code.
(concrete AI-assisted coding examples to come)
There’s a whole world beyond just frontend and “design engineering”. Back then the job of a frontend engineer could be as simple as creating buttons and implementing UIs. But every day, the job market becomes more competitive and the expectations for what you should know grow. We can’t silo ourselves as just designers or engineers now. So, it’s important to understand the big picture of the software you’re building.
Don’t let your fear and laziness get in the way of your curiosity.
more of what Andrew Ng had to say:

”… This leads to better decisions in choosing your software stack, designing system architecture, designing your data store, testing, and so on. It also leads to much better outcomes than those for an inexperienced developer who vibe codes a solution without knowing the tradeoffs their coding agent is making — which will often be poor ones, because they don’t know what context to give their coding agent. Understanding software engineering fundamentals lets you make good tradeoffs by steering coding agents using the precise language of software engineering.
AI also gives you the opportunity to take on greater ownership and agency than before. You can identify interesting problems and opportunities, and execute to take advantage of them in responsible ways. Taking advantage of this opportunity requires knowing how to drive projects forward. For example, knowing when to quickly build an MVP to take to users for testing, and when to slow down and take longer in order to build more carefully.”

issue -> idea of potential solution -> verify -> fix
but now it just goes

museums.title: museums
museums.content:
thoughts
ongoing thoughts on museums and art
08-22-2026
viewing someone’s art is like getting a peek into their brain through their process. that’s why it’s interesting to see basquiat’s sketches or nam june paik’s scribbles on newspapers… they’re interesting people, so interesting that the art world places them on a pedestal and wants to keep picking their brain and put their findings on display.
that’s why it’s important to live and build character. not necessarily to create better art, but because living and building characters are markers of a life well lived. and a life well lived tends to serve as inspiration for interesting art.
08-09-2026
Thoughts on “Compression Line” by Michael Hezier… This one is interesting because it was originally a site-specific land art sculpture in California’s Mojave Desert. It’s a single long weathering steel structure buried in the earth. What’s causing the bowing at the center is the pressure from the surrounding soil pressing the metal walls inward. I don’t think it can be considered “site-specific” anymore because it was dismantled and transplanted from California to here in a rich person’s art museum in Maryland. Its no longer the same earth or soil. To me, its not the same artwork… I feel that “site-specific” entails the societal and environmental context surrounding an artwork, in this case location.

Glenstone acts like a neutral, white-walled gallery that is actually not a neutral backdrop, but a space designed to make the art object look eternal and decontextualized.

Artists like Hezier left the gallery altogether to react against this, so I find it ironic that this artwork has made it to a place like Glenstone.
05-27-2026
museums are like history books we can walk through

you're-too-insecure-in-yourself.title: you're too insecure in yourself
you're-too-insecure-in-yourself.content:
feedback
joe told me, “you’re too insecure in yourself” when i told him that i cared about making a good impression on my instructors at school.
it reminds me of the time that i was in tokyo with xin, shelby, and michael and i felt overly-sensitive to the strict societal norms and being perceived as the “ignorant foreigner”. when i expressed this to xin he told me to not mind it and to just do what i need to have a good time (of course, there’s many more layers to this, between being anxious vs. being an utter asshole, but that’s a can of worms for another time.)
time and time again people like xin, shelby, and joe remind me to just not give a fuck. maybe its good to live in blissful ignorance, even if i have to fake it. because being so sensitive can be crippling.
